title: AI Cystoscopy
abstract: Systematic review type: PRISMA-DTA systematic review with conditional bivariate meta-analysis (Reitsma model), with three co-primary units of analysis (patient / lesion / image) synthesised sepa-rately. Registration: OSF Registries. POPULATION Adults (≥18 years) undergoing white-light cystoscopy (flexible office cystoscopy, rigid cystoscopy or transurethral resection) for suspected bladder cancer (haematuria, suspicious imaging, positive cytology) or for surveillance after conservative treatment of non-muscle-invasive bladder can-cer (NMIBC). Clinical context (primary detection vs surveillance) is a pre-specified subgroup variable; “not reported” is coded as such. Eligible data: prospectively or retrospectively collected cystoscopic still images or videos from human patients, including publicly released datasets, provided the origin of the images is traceable to a clinical cohort. Exclusions: paediatric populations; upper urinary tract endosco-py (ureteroscopy); phantom, animal or fully synthetic image sets; cohorts in which the target condition is not a bladder tumour. INDEX TEST Any artificial-intelligence system trained on cystoscopic image or video data (classical ma-chine learning, convolutional, transformer or hybrid deep learning; classification, object detection, se-mantic/instance segmentation) applied to cystoscopic images or videos acquired under white light, to identify bladder tumours, and evaluated on data independent of model training. The defining criterion is the acquisition modality: white-light cystoscopy without optical filtering or exogenous contrast agent. Purely software-based transformations of white-light frames applied downstream of acquisition (e.g., simulated spectral or hyperspectral conversion) are considered part of the AI pipeline and are eligible, coded as a covariate; when a standard white-light arm is reported alongside, both are extracted. The model output must be binarisable (tumour vs non-tumour) at a stated decision rule so that a 2×2 table is extractable or algebraically reconstructible; segmentation or detection studies reporting only overlap or detection metrics (Dice, IoU, mAP) without a 2×2 table are retained for narrative synthesis only. Studies combining white-light with enhanced imaging (NBI, blue light/PDD) are eligible only if a white-light-specific 2×2 table can be extracted; otherwise excluded (no white-light-specific data). Exclusions: gen-eral-purpose multimodal large language models used without task-specific training on cystoscopy data; blue-light/photodynamic diagnosis or NBI as the sole acquisition modality; confocal laser endomicros-copy and optical coherence tomography; Raman and other spectroscopies; CT/MR virtual cystoscopy; AI for surgical-phase recognition, image enhancement, stitching or 3D reconstruction without diagnostic accuracy outcomes. REFERENCE STANDARD Positive cases: histopathology from biopsy or transurethral resection. Negative cases: histopathology, clinical follow-up, or cystoscopy judged normal by the urologist; the method of verification is recorded for each study. Studies whose negative cases rest on the urologist’s judgement alone are eligible and included in the main pool, and rated High risk of bias in the QUADAS-2 reference-standard domain; a pre-specified sen-sitivity analysis is restricted to studies with histologically or follow-up–verified negative cases (≥6 months). Datasets in which positive labels derive from expert visual annotation without histological confirmation are retained for narrative synthesis only. Exclusions: no reference standard; reference limited to another AI output. DIAGNOSIS OF INTEREST Urothelial carcinoma of the bladder, any stage (Ta, T1, ≥T2), including carcinoma in situ, versus non-tumoural findings (normal mucosa, inflammation/cystitis, post-resection scar, other benign lesions). Non-urothelial bladder malignancies are included when reported within a mixed tumour class and cod-ed. Secondary target: tumour grade (low vs high) as a separate estimand, meta-analysed if at least 4 studies provide a 2×2 table, otherwise synthesised narratively; stage/invasion prediction from white-light im-ages: narrative only. STUDY DESIGN Eligible: diagnostic accuracy studies (prospective or retrospective; cohort or case-control/“two-gate” designs, the latter with an anticipated QUADAS-2 High rating on patient selection); reader studies com-paring AI with urologists on the same test set; randomised trials comparing AI-supported with standard white-light endoscopy, whose between-arm accuracy data are handled under the comparative question; full-length peer-reviewed conference proceedings papers with methods and results. Exclusions: conference abstracts and conference reviews; reviews, editorials, letters, protocols and trial-registry entries without results; dataset descriptors without a diagnostic evaluation; case reports; non-human studies. OUTCOMES Primary: sensitivity and specificity with a reconstructible 2×2 table (TP, FP, FN, TN), extracted separate-ly for each unit of analysis (patient, lesion, image/frame); units are never pooled together. Secondary: AUC, PPV/NPV, DOR, likelihood ratios; AI vs urologist accuracy on the same test set; urolo-gist-with-AI vs urologist-alone; tumour-grade accuracy; clinical-impact outcomes from randomised trials (detection rate, missed lesions, procedure time) described narratively. For studies without a reconstructible 2×2 table, the corresponding author is contacted (initial e‑mail at day 0, reminder at day 5, cutoff at day 10; all attempts documented); if the data are not obtained, the study is included in the narrative synthesis only. PRE-SPECIFIED ANALYSES Bivariate random-effects (Reitsma) meta-analysis conducted separately for each of the three co-primary units of analysis (patient, lesion, image); all clinical contexts are combined in the principal pool of each unit, and clinical context (primary detection / surveillance / not reported) is analysed as a pre-specified subgroup variable (see below). Feasibility: at least 4 studies per pool → bivariate model; fewer than 4 → narrative synthesis. No unit is designated as the single primary result; the three pools are reported with equal status. One data point per study and per unit, selected by a pre-defined rule (authors’ pre-specified threshold or designated primary model, then the most rigorous validation regime providing a 2×2 table: external > hold-out > nested cross-validation > k-fold), never the best-performing configura-tion. One entry per independent test cohort in the quantitative pool: when several reports share the same patients, the report is selected by a pre-defined, performance-blind rule (original publication for public benchmark datasets; otherwise: exploitable 2×2 table and reference standard > most rigorous validation regime > most complete cohort description > largest test set in patients > most recent); the other reports are described narratively. The same trained system evaluated on distinct test cohorts con-tributes one data point per cohort. Comparative analysis AI vs urologist (same test set): bivariate model with test-type covariate if at least 4 paired studies (a within-study paired comparison, hence a lower threshold than for between-study covariates); narrative otherwise; QUADAS-C applied. Pre-specified subgroup variables: clinical context, acquisition setting (office flexible cystoscopy vs oper-ating-room rigid/TURBT), input type (still images vs video/real-time), validation regime (internal vs external), task type (classification / detection / segmentation), software-transformed vs standard white-light frames, lesion morphology (flat/CIS vs papillary), model architecture family (classical machine learning / convolutional / transformer or hybrid), and two-gate vs single-gate design. For each variable, every level containing at least 4 studies is pooled separately with the bivariate model and its summary sensitivity and specificity (with 95% confidence and prediction regions) reported; levels with fewer than 4 studies are described narratively. A formal test of the difference between levels is performed only when the variable is informative in at least 10 studies within the pool, by entering it as a covariate in the bivariate model; the same ≥10-study threshold governs univariable meta-regression on continuous study-level covariates (publication year, training-set size, prevalence). All subgroup and meta-regression analyses are declared exploratory. Sensitivity analyses: restriction to studies with verified negative cases (histology or follow-up ≥6 months); exclusion of QUADAS-2 overall High; exclusion of PROBAST+AI Analysis High; exclusion of two-gate designs; external-validation results only; alternative validation regime when several 2×2 tables are reported; leave-one-out; alternative report per shared cohort. Heterogeneity: 95% prediction region as the primary indicator, τ² for logit sensitivity and specificity in support, I² reported only if required and never interpreted alone. Publication bias: Deeks’ funnel-plot asymmetry test computed separately for each pool (one per unit of analysis) with at least 10 studies; otherwise a reasoned statement. TEMPORAL AND LANGUAGE FRAME No lower date limit. Search cutoff: to be fixed at OSF deposit. Lan-guage: English only. Peer-reviewed publications only; preprints excluded. CERTAINTY OF EVIDENCE GRADE approach for diagnostic test accuracy applied to each primary esti-mand (sensitivity and specificity, per unit of analysis, and per clinical context where a context-specific pooled estimate is available), with a summary-of-findings table expressing true/false positives and neg-atives per 1000 patients at pre-specified prevalences of 15% and 20%. METHODOLOGICAL QUALITY ASSESSMENT QUADAS-2 for all included studies; PROBAST+AI for stud-ies developing or validating an AI model; QUADAS-C for studies entering the comparati

title: DAR ‐ SAC : Dynamic Adaptive Regularization Soft Actor‐Critic
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper proposes the dynamic adaptive regularization soft actor‐critic (DAR‐SAC) framework. The framework is based on the SAC algorithm, which is a reinforcement learning framework incorporating dynamic environment detection and adaptive optimization, to address the fixed exploration noise stiffness of the traditional SAC algorithm in dynamic environments. For the problems of fixed exploration noise rigidity, strategy oscillation aggravation and Q‐value over‐estimation in traditional SAC algorithms in dynamic environments, this paper firstly introduces a dynamic environment detection module to enable the robot to distinguish dynamic environments, and then combines the hybrid regularization mechanism and adaptive gradient trimming to accelerate convergence while suppressing abrupt changes in the strategy. In the constructed 3D point cloud simulation environment, the DAR‐SAC algorithm achieves significantly higher cumulative rewards and lower collision rates compared with SAC, SARC, DDPG, and TD3 algorithms. To further evaluate the robustness of the proposed framework against non‐stationary environments, we conduct extensive comparisons with state‐of‐the‐art variants, including SAC with adaptive entropy scheduling (SAC + AES), distributional SAC with three refinements (DSAC‐T), and SAC with delayed actor updates and replay mixing (SAC + DA + RM). The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method exhibits superior path‐planning performance in complex static and dynamic environments.

title: Continual learning via ensemble-based depth-wise masked autoencoders for data quality monitoring in high-energy physics
abstract: Abstract Machine learning (ML) techniques have been demonstrated to improve the accuracy and efficiency of anomaly detection (AD) when compared to conventional methods. This has led to the adoption of ML for data quality monitoring (DQM) use cases in order to monitor the operation of certain systems to ensure that they are free of undesirable or potentially deleterious anomalies. For applications in the field of High-Energy physics (HEP), where detectors must operate in long-running, harsh environments, ML models used in DQM that have been trained on static datasets are bound to experience degraded performance due to distributional shifts that naturally occur in the incoming data streams, unless directly mitigated via the inclusion of continual ML techniques. This work introduces DepthViT, a lightweight masked autoencoder architecture that employs unique depth-wise embeddings and depth-wise attention, to perform computationally efficient AD tasks. A continual learning framework is developed in which DepthViT models trained on the most recent data streams are ensembled with older models to create a robust overall system which is more resilient to shifts in incoming data streams. When evaluated on occupancy maps from the Compact Muon Solenoid (CMS) hadron calorimeter across multiple data-taking campaigns, the proposed method maintains precision above 98.8% and a stable ratio of correct anomaly predictions to number of anomalies both under small and large distributional shifts. Beyond HEP, the same ensembling-based continual adaptation strategy can be directly applied to industrial monitoring environments where data also naturally evolve over time. This work therefore presents a path toward adaptive anomaly detection systems capable of sustained operation in dynamic data environments.

title: Adaptive wavelet-CNN-LSTM forecasting with Bayesian optimization and SHAP interpretability for short-term solar irradiance prediction in a hot arid climate
abstract: Abstract Short-term global horizontal irradiance (GHI) forecasting is essential for solar grid integration in hot arid sites due to atmospheric variability and dust aerosols. This study proposes a hybrid deep learning (DL) pipeline that combines Discrete Wavelet Transform (DWT), Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), and Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) layers for 15-min GHI forecasting at a site in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. Wavelet decomposition and model hyperparameters are jointly optimized using Optuna’s Bayesian search across 20 trials, and SHAP-based feature selection retains only the most informative predictors. Uncertainty is quantified through Monte Carlo dropout across 100 stochastic forward passes with a dropout rate of 0.2. The model is evaluated on 105,312 meteorological records using five-fold time-series cross-validation. Across all observations, the model achieves a mean RMSE of 6.62 ± 2.22 W/m 2 and an R 2 of 0.98 ± 0.01. Daytime-filtered evaluation (GHI > 50 W/m 2 ) yields a mean RMSE of 8.28 ± 1.45 W/m 2 and an R 2 of 0.961 ± 0.015, providing a more conservative estimate of forecasting accuracy during operationally relevant periods. The full pipeline reduces RMSE by 28–40% compared to ablated model variants and achieves a 47% reduction compared to the persistence baseline. The proposed pipeline delivers interpretable solar irradiance forecasting with calibrated uncertainty estimates suited for grid management applications at arid-climate sites.

title: History-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning for real-time robot navigation in dynamic industrial environments
abstract: The advent of deep reinforcement learning (DRL) has significantly advanced the capabilities of autonomous mobile robots (AMRs) in navigating complex and dynamic environments. However, existing DRL models often struggle in industrial settings characterized by their unpredictable and changing nature. To address this challenge, we propose a novel History-Aware Deep Reinforcement Learning (HA-DRL) framework designed to enhance AMRs’ navigation capabilities by incorporating historical context into the learning process. The HA-DRL framework enriches the decision-making process by leveraging past experiences, enabling robots to make informed decisions in real-time, thus improving navigation efficiency and safety. This research highlights the importance of historical context in developing more adaptable, efficient, and safe autonomous navigation systems for industrial applications. title: Femtosecond laser-induced cavitation seeds liquid-jet breakup beyond the Rayleigh-Plateau stability limit
abstract: The Rayleigh-Plateau instability predicts that infinitesimal perturbations of a liquid jet grow only for kR < 1, with kR = 1 marking the classical stability boundary. Here, we show that femtosecond-laser-induced cavitation generates a localized, impulsive recoil perturbation on a flowing liquid jet, enabling a two-dimensional map of jet breakup across the (kR, epsilon/R) plane. The perturbation's spacing (wavelength) and strength (amplitude) are set independently by the laser repetition rate and pulse energy, respectively. At low amplitudes, tuning the repetition rate recovers the classical Rayleigh-Plateau dispersion relation and its kR = 1 cutoff, while increasing the wavelength enables controlled generation of monodisperse droplet trains, bidisperse droplet populations, and ultimately isolated single droplets. Along the amplitude axis, low pulse energies produce a seed that amplifies only the imposed wavenumber, whereas above a critical energy Ec, the seed broadens to excite many wavenumbers simultaneously. At still higher amplitudes, we demonstrate deterministic breakup for kR > 1, extending to kR = 1.9, with laser-synchronized droplet production rates up to 0.2 MHz. These results establish localized femtosecond-laser-induced cavitation as a route to controlled Rayleigh-Plateau breakup both within and beyond the classical linear-stability boundary.

title: Context-Aware Error Mitigation Orchestration for Hybrid Quantum Reinforcement Learning on NISQ Systems
abstract: Quantum Reinforcement Learning (QRL) integrates reinforcement learning with parameterized quantum circuits and is a promising approach to combinatorial optimization. On Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum (NISQ) devices, however, decoherence, gate imperfections, and measurement errors reduce policy quality and make learning less reliable. Existing error mitigation techniques are generally applied as fixed corrections that do not adapt to changing noise conditions or to the evolving state of training. This work presents Adaptive Policy-Guided Error Mitigation (APGEM) as a context-aware orchestration layer of the hybrid quantum-classical training loop that dynamically selects the most suitable mitigation strategy during QRL training. APGEM evaluates Zero-Noise Extrapolation (ZNE), Probabilistic Error Cancellation (PEC), Clifford Data Regression (CDR), and Readout Error Mitigation (REM) using policy-level indicators, including quantum-state fidelity, policy entropy, cumulative reward, and approximation ratio, and integrates the selected strategy directly into the reinforcement learning loop. The framework is evaluated on the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP), a representative NP-hard problem in urban logistics, under a range of NISQ noise models and noise levels. APGEM consistently outperforms conventional static mitigation methods, reaches approximately 94% of the utility of an oracle strategy, maintains higher quantum-state fidelity as noise increases, and produces more stable learning behaviour throughout training. Ablation studies show that the framework learns context-aware mitigation policies that adapt to different noise environments and circuit execution conditions. These findings demonstrate that integrating adaptive error mitigation into the learning process substantially improves the robustness and reliability of QRL on NISQ hardware.

title: Neither Here Nor There: Cross-Lingual Representation Dynamics of Code-Mixed Text in Multilingual Encoders
abstract: Multilingual encoder-based language models are widely used for code-mixed analysis, yet their internal representations of code-mixed inputs -- and their relationship to the constituent languages -- remain poorly understood. Using Hindi-English as a case study, we construct a unified trilingual corpus of parallel English, Hindi (Devanagari), and Romanized code-mixed sentences. We then probe cross-lingual representation alignment in standard multilingual encoders and their code-mix-adapted variants using CKA, token-level saliency, and entropy-based uncertainty analysis. We find that while standard models align English and Hindi well, code-mixed inputs remain loosely connected to either language -- and that continued pre-training on code-mixed data improves English-code-mixed alignment at the cost of English-Hindi alignment. Interpretability analyses further reveal a clear asymmetry: models process code-mixed text through an English-dominant semantic subspace, while native-script Hindi provides complementary signals that reduce representational uncertainty. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a trilingual post-training alignment objective that brings code-mixed representations closer to both constituent languages simultaneously, yielding more balanced cross-lingual alignment and downstream gains on sentiment analysis and hate speech detection -- showing that grounding code-mixed representations in their constituent languages meaningfully helps cross-lingual understanding. Code is available at: https://github.com/debajyotimaz/tri_align_EMNLP_2026.

title: Supervised Classification of Civil Unrest-Related Posts in Twitter/X Data: Evidence from the CUT Dataset
abstract: Social media platforms provide rapid public reports during demonstrations, crises, and civil unrest, but the volume and noise of user-generated content make manual monitoring impractical. This retrospective text-classification study evaluated supervised machine learning models for identifying incident-related civil unrest posts using the Civil Unrest on Twitter (CUT) dataset. The dataset consisted of 4,381 manually annotated English-language Twitter posts collected from 42 countries between 2014 and 2019. The analysis used keyword-based collection, language filtering, crowdsourced annotation, unigram bag-of-words representation, class-balancing procedures reported for the dataset, and supervised classification. Five algorithms were evaluated on the selected balanced dataset: Naive Bayes, Support Vector Machine, Logistic Regression, Gradient Boosted Decision Trees, and Convolutional Neural Network, each with and without hashtag features. In the original distribution, 690 posts were incident-related and 3,691 were non-incident-related. Dataset 2, containing 6,978 observations with 27% incident-related and 73% non-incident-related posts, was selected because it produced stronger minority-class performance. Incident-related F1-scores ranged from 0.845 to 0.915, and AUC values ranged from 0.958 to 0.977. SVM Model 1, trained with hashtag features, achieved the highest incident-related F1-score (0.915). The findings suggest that supervised classification may provide a useful filtering layer for analyst-supported civil unrest monitoring. However, the framework was evaluated on historical batch data rather than in a prospective streaming setting; therefore, real-time validation, transparent governance, multilingual testing, and stronger ethical safeguards are required before operational deployment.

title: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE ADOPTION AND ADMINISTRATIVE DECISION-MAKING IN UNIVERSITY SPORTS MANAGEMENT IN RIVERS STATE, NIGERIA
abstract: This study found that AI adoption significantly predicted administrative decision-making and sports management efficiency among university sports administrators in Rivers State, Nigeria. The study adopted a cross-sectional correlational research design. The study involved sports administrators from the University of Port Harcourt, Rivers State University, Ignatius Ajuru University of Education, and Federal University of Environment and Technology. The estimated population was 160 sports administrators, from which a sample of 114 respondents was selected using the Taro Yamane formula. Eighty-nine completed questionnaires were retrieved, representing a 78% return rate. Data were collected using a structured questionnaire measuring AI adoption, administrative decision-making, and sports management efficiency. Descriptive statistics, including mean and standard deviation, were used to answer the research questions, while simple linear regression was employed to test the hypotheses at the 0.05 significance level. The findings showed that AI adoption had a strong perceived influence on administrative decision-making (grand mean = 3.03). Regression analysis further indicated that AI adoption significantly predicted administrative decision-making, R = .614, R² = .377, β = .614, F(1, 87) = 52.61, p < .001. AI adoption also demonstrated a strong perceived influence on sports management efficiency (grand mean = 3.06) and significantly predicted management efficiency, R = .638, R² = .407, β = .638, F(1, 87) = 59.72, p < .001. The study concludes that AI adoption represents a promising mechanism for improving decision quality and operational efficiency in university sports management. The study recommended, among other things, that university sports management adopt AI-supported administrative systems for planning, scheduling, information management, resource allocation, and monitoring of sporting programs.

title: A Pre-Registered Evaluation Framework for Architecture-Induced Cognitive Performance in Large Language Models
abstract: This protocol pre-registers a controlled benchmark designed to test whether the ALEX cognitive architecture produces measurable changes in analytical performance when applied to the same underlying large language model used in a baseline condition. ALEX is treated as an orchestration and governance architecture rather than as a separate foundation model. The benchmark therefore isolates architecture as the principal experimental variable. The study uses 120 tasks across 12 cognitive categories, paired baseline/ALEX responses, blinded and randomized A/B evaluation, a pre-specified 100-point ALEX Cognitive Quality Score (ACQS), explicit error penalties, category-level diagnostics, and pre-specified rules for statistical analysis, success, partial success, and failure. The protocol is deliberately symmetric: it rewards thesis falsification, uncertainty calibration, expectation-gap reasoning, regime awareness and disciplined assertion, but also penalizes excessive caution, unnecessary complexity, verbosity, generic risk enumeration, and failure to answer a well-posed question. The benchmark is intended to determine not merely whether ALEX produces different answers, but where, if anywhere, its architecture creates reproducible cognitive advantages or costs.

title: Constrained Decoding for Structural Error Suppression in Dependency Tree Generation with Large Language Models
abstract: Abstract— In the field of syntactic parsing, fine-tuning large language models to generate a sentence’s syntactic structure in bracket form is a promising approach. Existing fine-tuned models demonstrate high values of syntax parsing metrics; however, in some cases they generate an incorrect bracket sequence (for example, with an unbalanced number of opening and closing parentheses). Therefore, this study aims to develop a method to reduce the number of incorrectly generated sequences. A system of constraints has been introduced on the set of tokens generated at each stage of the large language model. The implemented method was tested on four fine-tuned models (adapted and non-adapted with 4 and 8 billion parameters) on the SynTagRus dependency tree dataset. For all models, the number of incorrectly generated sequences decreased. However, some sentences were not parsed, because the LLMs generated an excessively long token sequence and were interrupted. The code for this study is publicly available.

title: Teleseismic case identification results of the DiTing 0.1b phase-picking model
abstract: Phase-picking models are usually trained on regional waveforms, and their performance on teleseismic records requires further examination using real data. This study takes the DiTing 0.1b phase-picking model of the DiTing seismic large-model series as the study object and carries out a case-based test of teleseismic phase identification within the DTFlowPro framework, using 15 global earthquakes of M5.0～5.9 that occurred from 22 to 31 December 2024. Two detection branches, the native-sampling branch and a 20 Hz resampling branch, were built. The candidates were fused by taking the union of time-clustered picks. The two branches showed clear complementarity. For P phases, 286 stations produced detections in both branches, 179 only in the native-sampling branch, and 40 only in the 20 Hz branch. The corresponding numbers for the S phase were 29, 19, and 25. The fused detections exactly matched the union of the two branches, and the station detection rates increased to 12.03% for the P phase and 1.74% for the S phase, 0.94 and 0.45 percentage points higher than those of the best single branch. The fused P detection rate decreased from 74.19% at 0°～10° to 4.19% at 90°～100°, and the fused S detection rate decreased from 58.06% at 0°～10° to below 8% beyond 10°. Among the combinations of three association methods and three fixed-depth location objective functions, the combination of native sampling, robust residual iteration, and the weighted L2 norm produced the smallest median epicentral error of 23.66 km. The event-building program dtevent of DTFlowPro merged 1102 phase picks and 359 origin solutions into 15 earthquakes, with no missing, incorrectly merged, or incorrectly split catalog events. This case-based evaluation of 15 typical teleseismic earthquakes indicates that, under catalog-guided conditions, the DiTing 0.1b model provides usable identification of teleseismic P phases within 90°, while the identification of S phases and of P phases beyond 90° remains limited. Because these conclusions are based on a limited number of cases, they should not be extrapolated to an assessment of teleseismic monitoring capability.

title: Towards Hijacking Interactions in Virtual Reality
abstract: We identify and study a new Virtual Reality Interaction Manipulation (VRIM) attack, where a remote attacker takes control of a user's interaction with the VR system, by trapping the user inside a malicious app that masquerades as the full VR interface. Once trapped, the user's interactions with apps, services, and other users can be recorded and modified without their knowledge. We build a prototype of VRIM on Meta Quest headsets and conduct an IRB-approved user study to validate its feasibility and efficacy. We disclosed VRIM and potential defenses to Meta, who responded positively. Our work emphasizes the need for new security measures tailored to the unique immersive nature of VR systems.

title: When and how anthropomorphic AI avatars relate to user engagement intentions: roles of emotional connection, perceived authenticity and technological familiarity
abstract: Purpose This study examines when and how anthropomorphic AI service avatars shape user engagement intentions in digital commerce. Drawing primarily on computers are social actors (CASA) theory and using parasocial interaction (PSI) as a bounded interpretive lens, it examines emotional connection as an encounter-specific affective mechanism and perceived authenticity and technological familiarity as theoretically focal contingencies operating at different stages of the engagement process. Design/methodology/approach Study 1 employed a between-subjects experiment that manipulated higher versus lower levels of bundled visual-form anthropomorphism. Study 2 used a three-wave survey of online shoppers to re-examine the focal relationships in prior AI-avatar service encounters. Mediation, moderation, and conditional indirect associations were estimated using PROCESS with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. Findings Study 1 shows that higher visual-form anthropomorphism increases user engagement intention, with emotional connection accounting for a meaningful but partial share of the effect. Study 2 provides associative support for the core relationships, although the association between anthropomorphism and emotional connection is comparatively modest. Perceived authenticity strengthens the theoretically focal association between anthropomorphism and emotional connection, while technological familiarity strengthens the association between emotional connection and engagement intention. The findings indicate that emotional connection represents one mechanism among multiple affective, cognitive and evaluative pathways linking anthropomorphic AI avatars with engagement intentions. Originality/value This study advances interactive marketing research by identifying emotional connection as a meaningful but partial encounter-level mechanism linking AI-avatar anthropomorphism with engagement intentions. It further demonstrates that perceived authenticity and technological familiarity condition the theoretically focal stages of this process, while the dominant direct component highlights the need for a multiple-pathway, rather than exclusively affective, account of AI-avatar engagement.

title: Spontaneity and authorship: a Kantian account of human authorship in copyright law
abstract: Generative AI has revived a neglected question in copyright law: why must authors be human? Courts and copyright offices have largely answered through statutory interpretation, but the underlying jurisprudence remains underdeveloped. This article draws on Kant’s theory of publication and spontaneity to argue that copyright protects an imputable communicative act. A copyright work transcends its status as a produced object to exist fundamentally as a public address attributable to a rational subject capable of authorising its communication. The article grounds this account in the architecture of Kant’s Doctrine of Right: the mandate that authorises publication is a relation between persons, modelled on the Roman mandatum, and the standing from which it issues is an exercise of the author’s innate right of communicative freedom. Current AI systems possess the capacity to generate outputs, yet they remain incapable of originating communicative acts or issuing mandates in the Kantian sense. The article further develops a Mandate Test for human-AI collaboration and concludes that the human authorship requirement follows from the nature of authorship itself, not merely from historical practice or legislative convention.

evidence.abstract: Generative AI has revived a neglected question in copyright law: why must authors be human? Courts and copyright offices have largely answered through statutory interpretation, but the underlying jurisprudence remains underdeveloped. The article further develops a Mandate Test for human-AI collaboration and concludes that the human authorship requirement follows from the nature of authorship itself, not merely from historical practice or legislative convention.

title: Ultra-short-term PV power prediction based on a dual-stream CNN-GRU-attention framework
abstract: Aiming at the challenges of data noise and cumulative error in photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting, this paper proposes a dat a and model dual-closed-loop ultra-short-term forecasting framework. At the data end, the interquartile range (IQR) method and forward-backward interpolation are utilized to reconstruct outliers, while the Spearman coefficient and sine-cosine encoding are combined to optimize meteorological and temporal features. At the model end, a dual-stream network is constructed using a multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) strategy. The historical stream extracts multi-scale temporal features using a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) - Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) - Attention mechanism, whereas the future stream resolves weather trends using a GRU. Simulation results show that the model's coefficient of determination reaches 0.983, and simulation comparisons with other models and ablation studies have demonstrated the superiority of the proposed model and the effectiveness of its core components.

title: Hesitation Has a Geometry: Entropy-Trained Hyperbolic Probes for Sparse Activation Steering
abstract: When a large language model solves a mathematical problem, its reasoning is largely hierarchical, and the solution often branches at a few tokens where the next-token entropy is high. Such tree-like structure embeds in hyperbolic space with far lower distortion than in Euclidean space. Activation steering, however, usually edits the hidden states of a pretrained model by adding one fixed Euclidean vector at every token, even though most tokens of a solution are already determined by the context. We propose Hyperbolic Entropy Steering (HEST), which embeds the hidden states in the Poincaré ball with a lightweight probe whose only label is the model's own next-token entropy. Where this entropy exceeds a threshold, HEST moves the embedded state along the geodesic of steepest descent of a readout of the probe and maps the change back to the hidden state. For the Busemann readout of a learned ideal point, we prove that a step of fixed length lowers it by the same amount at every state. On three instruction-tuned models from the Qwen2.5-Math and Llama-3.1 families, HEST with the Busemann readout improves greedy accuracy on MATH-500 and GSM8K in five of six settings, by up to 1.8 points, whereas a contrastive steering vector added at every token lowers accuracy. With a Euclidean probe trained in the same way, this gain disappears on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B-Instruct. The gains are largest on problems where the model hesitates often, and accuracy on the remaining problems is almost unchanged.

title: DeskForge: Dense Supervision from Desktop Environments for Computer-Use Agents
abstract: Computer-use agents need to reliably ground action targets in complex desktop scenes, where multiple applications, overlapping windows, and visually similar controls compete for attention. Existing training data rarely pair such scenes with dense annotations or vary them in a controlled way. We introduce DeskForge, a controllable desktop environment that composes and explores real applications to generate large-scale supervision for computer-use agents. It varies application states, content, window layout, appearance, and resolution, and fuses screenshots, accessibility trees, and window geometry into dense element annotations while recording the outcome of each executed action. Using this environment, we construct DeskForge-1M, a corpus of 1.2M annotated desktop observations containing 159.7M element instances. We fine-tune four vision-language models on 200K grounding examples drawn from DeskForge-1M. All four improve across held-out desktop conditions and on all five external GUI grounding benchmarks; for Qwen3.5-4B, accuracy increases by 11.51 percentage points on ScreenSpot-Pro and 10.11 points on OSWorld-G. The gains also translate to long-horizon task completion: under a fixed planner, the fine-tuned action models solve more WebArena-Infinity and OpenApps tasks, with Qwen3.5-4B increasing from 31 to 50 of 119 tasks and from 3 to 15 of 100 tasks, respectively. These results show that controllable composition of real desktop environments provides a scalable source of supervision for improving both GUI grounding and long-horizon computer use. The framework code, the dataset, and the fine-tuned model are available from the project page: https://saidgurbuz.github.io/deskforge/

title: Before It Fades: Reinforcing Temporal Representations at Inference Time in VideoLLMs
abstract: Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) receive frames in sequential order and interpret how visual content evolves along the temporal axis, yet temporal reasoning remains a persistent weakness across architectures. Reversing the frame order of a video, a transformation that should invert temporal answers, often leaves the final prediction unchanged. We investigate where this failure originates by defining the temporal divergence vector τ_l, the layer-wise representational difference induced by reversing temporal order. Tracking its magnitude across layers reveals a consistent temporal divergence profile where the divergence peaks at intermediate layers and progressively diminishes toward the output. We confirm this peak is specific to temporal reasoning and functionally critical for predictions, establishing that VideoLLMs acquire temporal information at intermediate layers but fail to maintain it to the output. This progressive fading motivates our method, Temporal Activation Injection (TAI), which extracts τ_l at the peak of the profile for each input and reinjects it into subsequent layers following the measured decay. TAI requires no training and consistently improves temporal reasoning across three VideoLLMs and four benchmarks with negligible impact on non-temporal tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/Youngwoo-git/Before-It-Fades.

title: Know When to Hold 'em: Correct-Token Retention in Uniform-State Diffusion Language Models
abstract: Uniform-state diffusion models (USDMs) can revise any token at any denoising step, which lets them correct their own mistakes, a key advantage over masked diffusion. Self-correction, however, requires both revising incorrect tokens and retaining correct ones, and we show that current USDMs lack the latter. Even under greedy-tail decoding, state-of-the-art USDMs (DUO, UDLM, and uniform-noise SEDD) keep revising 173--270 of 512 positions at every step, and these large, uncoordinated edits collapse sample diversity. A random-token corruption experiment traces this deficit to the models themselves: they reconstruct clean and corrupted tokens with nearly identical accuracy, even though clean tokens are easier targets. A decomposition of the validation NELBO shows that training barely rewards retention: incorrect predictions are heavily penalized at corrupted positions but almost free at clean ones. We propose Correct-Token Retention Regularization (CTR-Reg), a simple but effective auxiliary loss that trains the model to retain tokens left unperturbed by the forward process and requires no change to the sampler. CTR-Reg improves clean-token accuracy by 26.5 percentage points on average across six benchmarks, while leaving corrupted-token accuracy virtually unchanged, and its per-step revisions converge to only 3--11 positions. With just five greedy-tail steps, generative perplexity more than halves under CTR-Reg for all three models while diversity is preserved, and these gains hold across sampling budgets. Our results identify correct-token retention as a key missing ingredient for self-correcting diffusion language models, and demonstrate an effective fix.

title: A Quantum Phase Neural Network with Multi-Inputs/Single-Output
abstract: A 35 input/single output quantum phase neural network (QPNN) is proposed to recognize the English letters' A 'and' B 'composed 7*5 of pixels. Each node of the proposed QPNN has the input with 0 or 1. Through normalization and quantum phase encoding, each set of 35 with 0 or 1 digital inputs is encoded into a quantum superposition state described by 35 quantum phases. Then, a quantum rotation gate is used to introduce adjustable phase, and a controlled NOT gate is used to entangle the relative phase between the two inputs. The relationship between the input and output of the network is derived. This paper also derived the phase weight learning training algorithm with adaptive learning rate. The solutions with the recognition probability of 1 is designed, and the analytical expressions for all adjustable phase solutions with zero errors are not unique. The experimental performance is verified on the Qiskit platform. This paper uses phase drive to convert the probability calculation into an analytical polynomial function with adjustable rotation angles in the network, avoiding the bottleneck of generating all 2^35 complex exponential amplitudes and providing an effective way to solve the "exponential wall" problem, which provides a new implementation solution for the practical application of multi-input recognition problems.

title: RVCBench: Benchmarking the Robustness of Voice Cloning Across Modern Audio Generation Models
abstract: Modern Voice Cloning (VC) can synthesize speech that closely matches a target speaker from only seconds of reference audio, enabling applications such as personalized speech interfaces and dubbing. In practical deployments, modern audio generation models inevitably encounter noisy reference audios, imperfect text prompts, multilingual and long-form generation settings, downstream post-processing, and adversarial perturbations, all of which can significantly hurt robustness. Despite rapid progress in VC driven by autoregressive codec-token language models and diffusion-based models, robustness under realistic deployment shifts remains underexplored. This paper introduces RVCBench, a comprehensive dataset and benchmark that evaluates Robustness in Voice Clone. RVCBench contributes a large-scale, task-aligned robustness dataset that instantiates realistic deployment shifts through controlled text-audio pairing, multilingual and long-form scenarios, expressive prompts, post-processing conditions, and passive or proactive audio perturbations. Covering 18 robustness evaluations, 204 unique speakers, and 14,370 utterance-level evaluation items, RVCBench enables unified evaluation of input sensitivity, generation stability, output resilience, and perturbation robustness. We evaluate 18 representative modern open-source VC models and reveal systematic vulnerabilities in content consistency, speaker similarity, long-form stability, post-processing resilience, adversarial robustness, and detector-facing separability. We open-source the toolkit and dataset to support reproducible evaluation and future research.

title: Lifting the maximally-entangledness assumption in robust self-testing for synchronous games
abstract: Robust self-testing in non-local games allows a classical referee to certify that two untrustworthy players are able to perform a specific quantum strategy up to high precision. Proving robust self-testing results becomes significantly easier when one restricts the allowed strategies to symmetric projective maximally entangled (PME) strategies, which allow natural descriptions in terms of tracial von Neumann algebras. This has been exploited in the celebrated M I P ∗ = R E paper and related articles to prove robust self-testing results for synchronous games when restricting to PME strategies. However, the PME assumptions are not physical, so these results need to be upgraded to make them physically relevant. In this work, we do just that: we prove that any perfect synchronous game which is a robust self-test when restricted to PME strategies, is in fact a robust self-test for all strategies. We then apply our result to the Quantum Low Degree Test to find an efficient n -qubit test.

title: Construction of a Teaching Quality Monitoring and Evaluation System Based on Data Mining Analysis
abstract: In our country, the teacher team construction and management level are constantly improving. It is crucial to enhance education quality, particularly classroom teaching quality. This study explores the application of data mining techniques in teaching quality evaluation. Using a dataset comprising evaluation scores from 10 teachers at a university, we construct a prototype system to demonstrate the proposed methodology, this paper studied the large data mining technology and clustering analysis algorithm, and based on this algorithm, put forward the teaching quality control and evaluation system, and choose a college teacher to students train the system, finally, the application of this system, the application effect is good. The specific conclusions are as follows: (1) compared with Apriori algorithm, FP-growth algorithm and HBE-Apriori algorithm, this algorithm has obvious advantages in operation speed. (2) The theoretical basis of K-mean clustering and the method of evaluating K-mean clustering are given, specific procedures and implementation procedures are given, and finally an example is given to illustrate its process and operation process. There are many ways of evaluation, with an emphasis on analyzing the values of purity and F1. (3) expounds three levels of the platform: performance level, service level and data level. Then, the specific implementation schemes of system initialization design, data collection, data preprocessing and data mining are expounded. (4) There is a close connection between teachers ’education quality and students’ education quality. The corresponding “satisfaction” of “excellent” teachers is 0.8; the education quality of teachers is “good”; if the teaching content is good and the level evaluation confidence is 0.7, the confidence level is 0.5 regardless of whether the level evaluation is satisfactory or basically satisfied, significantly lower than both “good” and “level evaluation”. Another important element is the reasonable arrangement and optimization of the course content. This study employed evaluation scores from ten faculty members at a university as a preliminary pilot dataset to demonstrate the proposed methodological workflow, thereby constructing a prototype system. We explicitly acknowledge that this sample size constitutes the primary limitation of the study, and the generalizability of the conclusions requires further validation. When teaching content is rated as ’excellent,’ the confidence level for a ’satisfactory’ evaluation grade is 0.7; when teaching content is rated as ’good,’ the confidence level for both ’satisfactory’ and ’basically satisfied’ evaluations is 0.5—significantly lower than the level for ’excellent’ teaching content.

title: A comparative study of GCN and GraphSAGE algorithms for structural anomaly detection in public procurement networks
abstract: Bid rigging and procurement collusion may produce structural patterns in the relationships between companies and procurement opportunities. This study compares Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) and GraphSAGE for structural anomaly detection in a heterogeneous company–tender procurement network. The study uses Government Procurement via GeBIZ data from Singapore and introduces controlled synthetic anomalies because the dataset does not provide complete bidder-participation information or verified collusion labels. A leakage-aware temporal evaluation is applied together with multiple anomaly difficulties, random seeds, unseen anomaly subjects, and cross-pattern testing. The results show different empirical behavior between the two architectures. GraphSAGE achieves higher F1-Score, ROC-AUC, and PR-AUC in the multi-seed evaluation, while GCN achieves higher recall. GraphSAGE also performs better in the true inductive evaluation on unseen anomaly subjects. An Early Warning System based on GraphSAGE is further developed to rank companies according to their structural anomaly scores. The findings indicate that graph-based models can support structural anomaly screening, while synthetic anomaly results should not be interpreted as evidence of confirmed procurement collusion.

title: Artificial Intelligence: A Beginner's Guide
abstract: Artificial Intelligence: A Beginner's Guide provides an accessible introduction to the fundamental concepts, technologies, and applications of Artificial Intelligence. The book explains essential topics such as intelligent systems, machine learning, deep learning, neural networks, natural language processing, computer vision, robotics, and Generative AI in a clear and easy-to-understand manner. It introduces readers to how AI systems learn from data, recognize patterns, make predictions, and support decision-making across diverse domains. The book also explores practical applications of AI in healthcare, education, finance, business, transportation, and everyday technology while addressing important considerations related to ethics, privacy, security, and responsible AI. Designed for beginners, students, educators, and aspiring professionals, the book provides a strong foundation for exploring the rapidly evolving world of Artificial Intelligence.

title: Unmanned Underwater Vehicle Path Following Based on Improved Soft ActorCritic with Action Smoothing
abstract: The deep reinforcement learning (DRL) method shows great potential in unmanned underwater vehicle (UUV) motion control. Traditional control methods rely on an accurate UUV model. However, due to the nonlinearity of the UUV model and the complex underwater environment, it is difficult to obtain an accurate model in practice. Therefore, we propose a DRL-based path-following control method for UUV. Specifically, this method integrates the Soft Actor–Critic (SAC), prioritized experience replay (PER), and policy smoothing methods to improve the generalization, tracking accuracy, and smoothness of the controller. PER assigns greater sampling weights to samples with high learning efficiency. Another major challenge in the UUV control problem arises from the action oscillations induced by the DRL policy. This problem leads to excessive wear of the actuator system and difficulty in practical applications. To address this, an improved policy regularization method is designed to promote action smoothness. evidence.title: Unmanned Underwater Vehicle Path Following Based on Improved Soft ActorCritic with Action Smoothing
evidence.abstract: The deep reinforcement learning (DRL) method shows great potential in unmanned underwater vehicle (UUV) motion control. Traditional control methods rely on an accurate UUV model. However, due to the nonlinearity of the UUV model and the complex underwater environment, it is difficult to obtain an accurate model in practice. Therefore, we propose a DRL-based path-following control method for UUV. Specifically, this method integrates the Soft Actor–Critic (SAC), prioritized experience replay (PER), and policy smoothing methods to improve the generalization, tracking accuracy, and smoothness of the controller. PER assigns greater sampling weights to samples with high learning efficiency. Another major challenge in the UUV control problem arises from the action oscillations induced by the DRL policy. This problem leads to excessive wear of the actuator system and difficulty in practical applications. To address this, an improved policy regularization method is designed to promote action smoothness. In addition, a dynamic reward function that integrates tracking error, motion state, and control signals is designed to improve training efficiency. The simulation results show that improved SAC has a smooth control signal and good tracking accuracy in different waypoint configurations and uncertain disturbances.

title: Programming with Composable Recursive Patterns and Transformations
abstract: Data processing using traditional pattern matching syntax and direct recursive functions is straightforward to write but becomes awkward in ambiguous (i.e., nondeterministic) cases: when programmers wish to avoid backtracking, they often end up having to write complicated code that sacrifices clarity and modularity. However, when the tree language being matched is regular, better solutions are possible. This paper presents composable recursive patterns and transformations (CRPTs), a new programming language feature designed to tackle this problem. CRPTs resemble and act like recursive type definitions in a structurally-typed language, which can be composed seamlessly to type check programs, but they also have a runtime component: they are compiled into backtracking-free code that recognizes and transforms their input in linear time. They serve both to validate existing data—for example, when checking structured JSON input against a CRPT that acts as a data schema—and to transform data in a type-safe and efficient manner. We formalize the dynamic semantics of CRPTs, a static type system for them, and a translation into efficient code that executes in time linear in the size of the input and polynomial in the size of the pattern. We also demonstrate the practicality of CRPTs with an implementation in the MLscript programming language, which we evaluate against comparable existing approaches on several examples.

title: Refined² Environment Classifiers
abstract: MetaML-style multi-stage programming (MSP) supports quasi-quotation-based code generation, runtime execution of generated code, and cross-stage persistence (CSP). However, its interaction with computational effects is subtle: mutable state can cause scope extrusion, where generated code escapes the scope of variables on which it depends. This paper presents a type system for MetaML-style MSP with mutable state that statically rules out harmful scope extrusion while supporting multi-level code generation, runtime execution, and a variant of CSP. Our system builds on refined environment classifiers (RECs), a discipline that annotates code types with the variable scopes on which generated code depends. To scale RECs to the MetaML-style setting, we refine classifiers so that they track not only variable scopes, but also the scopes of classifiers themselves. Further, we integrated polymorphism over classifiers, enabling more general and reusable code generation patterns in a multi-level setting. For the resulting system, we define an operational semantics via a definitional interpreter and prove type soundness and safety of offline code generation, showing that generated code can be extracted as standalone well-typed programs. We provide working implementations and mechanized proofs in Rocq.

title: VFedHeal: heterogeneity-aware vertical federated learning with dynamic privacy scheduling for personalized healthcare sensing
abstract: Abstract Vertical federated learning (VFL) can combine aligned medical and wearable data without pooling raw features, but fixed synchronization wastes communication under device heterogeneity, repeated exchanges expose private information, and population models transfer poorly across individuals. We propose VFedHeal, a personalized healthcare VFL system that integrates delay-aware FedBCD, dynamic budget scheduling differential privacy (DBS-DP), and chronological subject calibration. The scheduler assigns faster parties more local updates and sets synchronization intervals from measured processing times. DBS-DP clips exchanged representations and adds Gaussian noise on a public schedule; its fixed zero-concentrated differential privacy budget yields an explicit privacy bound for each party. For a new participant, VFedHeal retains encoders learned from other participants and adjusts only three class-bias parameters using a small set of early labeled trials. Experiments on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and NUS-WIDE assess convergence and inference resistance; AFFEC and WESAD test multimodal physiological sensing. On AFFEC, subject-calibrated VFL achieved a macro- F 1 of 0.478, compared with 0.475 for centralized fusion. End-to-end VFedHeal achieved a macro- F 1 of 0.471 with 47.5% less communication than personalized vanilla VFL. The scheduler reduced communication by 51.9% on WESAD. The proposed framework supports personalized healthcare VFL with adaptive coordination and privacy schedules calibrated to the target cohort and sensing modalities.

title: Automatic classification of participants’ role in cyberbullying
abstract: Cyberbullying is the evolution of bullying over an electronic medium. Most existing studies focus on detecting cyberbullying by analyzing the textual content of interactions. Yet, the interaction between participants in cyberbullying conversations was poorly understood as most studies disregard content from victims and bystanders and focus on the bully. This study aimed to develop and evaluate model for identifying cyberbullying participants' roles, including harassers, victims, and bystander defenders, thus broadening the scope to encompass all interaction roles. Conventional Machine Learning (CML) and Transfer Learning (TL) methods were employed on the AMiCA English dataset, which encompasses a broad spectrum of cyberbullying scenarios and detailed role annotations. We conducted a comparative analysis of different techniques to select the most effective model. A comparative analysis of various techniques was performed to identify the most effective model. CML approach incorporated various feature sets includes textual, embedding, sentiment and emotional, psycholinguistics and toxicity features, as well as term lists. With newly integrated toxicity and brand-new psycholinguistics features, Linguistic Inquiry and Word (LIWC) 2022 and Empath, this study set a new benchmark for role identification. Contextual embeddings from ggeluBert, tnBert, and DistilBert achieved noteworthy results, with DistilBert emerging as the most effective across role classes. Feature engineering revealed that textual features and DistilBert embeddings, both independently and in combination, offered the most predictive power. The overall CML models effectiveness was improved when provided with diverse feature combinations, with Multinomial Logistic Regression (MLR) outperformed Linear Support Vector Classifier (SVC). TL approaches using fine-tuned Pre-trained Language Models (PLMs) like DistilBert, DistilRoBerta, and Electra-small outperformed CML models, with optimized DistilBert yielding the highest macro F-measure of 70.6% achieving about 10 percentage points (p.p) increase in performance compared to existing benchmarks and improved recall score across all role classes. This improvement underscores the state-of-the-art PLMs to more effectively identify and differentiate the nuanced roles of participants in cyberbullying scenarios. Additionally, a Streamlit application was developed to detect and classify the roles of participants. However, the models in this study currently classify only English text, limiting their broader linguistic applicability. Future work could explore new directions, including sarcasm detection to address contextual overlaps in harasser and victim messages, expanding the framework to capture interactional dynamics between posts, and adapting it for multilingual and multimodal data.

title: Multi‐Strategy Snow Ablation Optimizer for Global Optimization
abstract: ABSTRACT The snow ablation optimizer (SAO) is a novel meta‐heuristic algorithm inspired by the natural processes of snow melting and sublimation. SAO employs a dual‐population dynamic adjustment mechanism to balance exploration and exploitation, demonstrating significant performance in global optimization. However, when dealing with complex optimization problems, the SAO algorithm tends to suffer from low convergence accuracy and premature convergence. To address these issues, this paper proposes a multi‐strategy snow ablation optimizer (MSSAO). Firstly, it adopts an external archive mechanism to prevent convergence to local optima. Secondly, it utilizes an adaptive t ‐distribution perturbation strategy to achieve a balance between exploration and exploitation. Finally, it employs a mirror reflection learning strategy to maintain population diversity. Comprehensive experiments conducted on the CEC2017 and CEC2022 test suites demonstrate that MSSAO significantly enhances both global optimization performance and convergence accuracy. Furthermore, its effectiveness in engineering optimization is demonstrated through a DC motor control system.

title: When Terminal-Agent Training Stalls: Demystifying Data Generation and Verification Challenge
abstract: Using a frontier model like Claude Opus as a meta-agent to generate terminal tasks and verifiers for RL training is increasingly common. Yet a runnable Docker image and executable test suite do not guarantee a faithful end-to-end pipeline for terminal agent training. We present a meta-agent pipeline motivated by this gap, diagnosing three classes of failure: benchmark invalidity, harness brittleness, and reward misalignment. Prompt redesign and context extension raise baseline solvability 5.6 times, but a 9B model saturates at 81.3% mean pass@2 within 20 steps on Claude Opus-generated tasks. Adding hard tasks reduces mean pass@2 to 20.6% without changing the training configuration, a strong evidence that the solvability band is model-specific. These findings demonstrate that meta-agent reliability requires solvability-band calibration, verifier audits, and infrastructure error accounting as first-class evaluation criteria, not post-hoc diagnost.

title: Point spread function requirements for dark matter subhalo detection with the Habitable Worlds Observatory
abstract: Different theories of dark matter predict different populations and morphologies of galactic subhaloes below about 10^8M_{odot}. The planned angular resolution and optical stability of the Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) should enable it to detect subtle subhalo perturbations in strongly lensed galaxy images. We simulate 2000-second exposures with its High Resolution Imager (HRI) under the fiducial Exploratory Analytic Case 1 (EAC1) design, assuming known source structure and omitting lens-galaxy light. Pre-selecting the top 50 of 965 lenses (5.2%) using only arc signal-to-noise and relative gradient power lowers the median mass threshold for 10% aperture coverage roughly tenfold relative to the full ensemble. The top 12 (1.2%) reach a median of 6.6times10^7M_{odot} for the same coverage. At their most sensitive positions, the top 50 and top 12 reach median thresholds of 3times10^7M_{odot} and 1.5times10^7M_{odot}, respectively. Non-linear fits support the Fisher forecasts at the tested masses and positions. For these 12 lenses, increasing the physical wavefront error from 35 to 65 nm RMS raises the median thresholds by only 0.1 dex when the point spread function (PSF) is modelled correctly. Deliberately mismodelling the 35-nm reference PSF removes detectable positions, although false detections remain rare. Under our illustrative retention criteria, loss of sensitive area sets a median tolerated wavefront mismatch of 5 nm RMS (range 2--10 nm). Selective HWO follow-up of lenses discovered by Euclid or Roman could therefore transform our understanding of the nature of dark matter, provided that the PSF is characterized accurately enough to preserve this sensitivity.

title: Sparse Hamiltonian simulation with optimal dependence on the maximum column Euclidean norm
abstract: We give a quantum algorithm for simulating a $d$-sparse Hermitian Hamiltonian $H$, assuming a known upper bound $Λ$ on its maximum column Euclidean norm $\|H\|_{1\to2}$. For $tΛ\ge1/2$, simulation with operator-norm error $ε$ uses \[ O\!\left(tΛ\sqrt d+\sqrt d\log(2/ε)\right) \] sparse-oracle queries. This removes the subpolynomial overhead in Low's algorithm [STOC 2019], replacing it with an additive logarithmic precision term. For $d>1$ and $tΛ\ge\log(2/ε)$, the bound matches the worst-case lower bound. A known spectral-norm upper bound may also be used in place of $Λ$. The number of 1- and 2-qubit gates is linear in the query scale, up to oracle costs and polynomial overhead in the input bit lengths and logarithmic precision parameters. As applications, we obtain $O(κ\sqrt d\,\mathrm{polylog}(κ/ε))$ queries for solving $d$-sparse quantum linear systems with $\|A\|\le1$ and $\|A^{-1}\|\leκ$, under standard sparse and state-preparation access. We also give a gate-efficient implementation of black-box unitaries with at most $d$ nonzero entries per row and column using $O(\sqrt d\log(2/ε))$ queries, given sparse access to the unitary and its adjoint. At constant error, the query bound is optimal and yields $Θ(\sqrt N)$ queries for arbitrary $N\times N$ unitaries, resolving the open question on black-box unitary implementation posed by Berry and Childs [QIC 2012].

title: Code Owns the Simulation, Jev Owns the Evaluation
abstract: Judgment models such as \jev{} return, in a single call and without reasoning text, a probability for each described option. This makes them attractive as an agent's action-selection layer, but it is unclear which decisions they can be trusted with. We test \jev{} on reflection tests, one-shot matrix games, the text game ALFWorld and robot control, and find a sharp boundary. \jev{} succeeds when the right option can be judged from what the input describes, which we call \emph{evaluation}. Specifically, it solves 99\% of the counterintuitive Cognitive Reflection Test questions. However, it fails when the right option depends on \emph{simulation} (i.e., predicting something not in the input), such as the opponent's action or the subgoal that must come first. In games, \jev{} plays suboptimally as if its rational opponent acted at random, because the opponent's action is not given. In ALFWorld, \jev{} favors commands that mention an object or place named in the task description. For example, given the task ``put a clean knife in the drawer'', \jev{} carries an unwashed knife straight to the drawer instead of first washing it at the sink. Surprisingly, many of these failures are not due to a lack of knowledge. Asked separately what the opponent will do, \jev{} usually answers correctly, and it responds well given the opponent's action. It fails when one call must both perform the simulation and evaluate based on it. This suggests letting code make the prediction or simulation. When code supplies it, such as a lookahead in ALFWorld and physics simulation in robot control, \jev{} becomes an expert controller through its general evaluation ability.

title: Non-Markovian effects on informational steady states
abstract: Informational steady states (ISSs) arise when the rate at which information is gained from continuous measurements is exactly balanced by the rate at which information from earlier measurements is lost to the environment. While ISSs have been studied in Markovian settings, relatively little is known about how memory effects influence their formation and steady-state properties. In this work, we investigate non-Markovian effects on ISSs within the framework of continuously monitored collision models. We model the environment as a sequence of two-qubit ancillas and find that, for this specific model, the steady-state information gain per measurement is negatively correlated with the degree of non-Markovianity. Numerical results further characterize how the system-ancilla and ancilla-ancilla interaction parameters influence both the degree of non-Markovianity and the steady-state information gain.

title: Mass-asymmetry-controlled exciton dressing and dissociation in a quantum lattice model
abstract: In a polar material, a neutral exciton couples to phonons through the sum of the electron and hole deformation potentials. Because the total source vanishes by charge neutrality, the elastic exciton-phonon vertex is regularized by electron-hole interference. Here we determine the non-perturbative fate of this interference by exact diagonalization of a Holstein-exciton model. By parameterizing the mass asymmetry to decouple it from the small-polaron atomic limit, we map a regime map comprising an internal dressing crossover and a dissociation boundary. We prove analytically and verify numerically that for equal masses, the symmetric exciton ground state is protected from phonon dressing by an exact exchange selection rule, provided the phonon source is odd under electron-hole exchange (the neutral case). As mass asymmetry increases, this selection rule is broken and the exciton acquires a strong local polaronic cloud. We show that the dissociation boundary, conversely, is set by a global energy balance between Coulomb binding and polaronic stabilization, and is nearly independent of the internal dressing. Paradoxically, the very symmetry that protects the exciton from dressing denies it polaronic stabilization, driving it toward dissociation at strong coupling. We discuss these results in the context of lattice exciton-polaron models and their implications for sharp versus broad excitonic lines in mass-symmetric versus mass-asymmetric polar semiconductors.

title: Geometric Stability: The Missing Axis of Representations
abstract: Representational similarity methods compare the geometries of neural representations, but they do not measure how consistently the geometry of a single representation is recovered from subsets of its feature coordinates. We call this property geometric stability and introduce Shesha, which estimates it by correlating representational dissimilarity matrices from complementary random feature subsets. Shesha is not invariant to orthogonal rotations: representations with identical Gram matrices, and therefore identical linear CKA, can have different geometric stability. Controlled transformations further separate the quantities. Across 2{,}463 encoder configurations spanning seven domains, similarity and stability are positively associated across non-PCA transformations (ρ=+0.75) but negatively associated under PCA-coordinate compression (ρ=-0.47). We further evaluate 170 pretrained vision models across six datasets. DINOv2 combines strong transfer performance with bottom-quartile stability on five of six datasets, showing that transferability and feature-split stability need not coincide. Across random feature subsets, the marginal relationship between Shesha and linear-probe variability is dataset-dependent; after controlling for task alignment with LogME, higher Shesha is associated with lower variability on five of six datasets. These results identify geometric stability as a basis-dependent property that complements representational similarity and task alignment.

title: Fast Wasserstein rates for estimating probability distributions of probabilistic graphical models
abstract: Using i.i.d. data to estimate a high-dimensional distribution in Wasserstein distance is a fundamental instance of the curse of dimensionality. We explore how structural knowledge about the data-generating process, which gives rise to the distribution can be used to overcome this curse. More precisely, we work with the set of distributions of probabilistic graphical models for a given directed acyclic graph. It turns out that this knowledge is only helpful if it can be quantified, which we formalize via smoothness conditions on the transition kernels in the disintegration corresponding to the graph. In this case, we prove that the rate of estimation is governed by the local structure of the graph, more precisely by dimensions corresponding to single nodes together with their parent nodes. The precise rate depends on the exact notion of smoothness assumed for the kernels, where either weak (Wasserstein–Lipschitz) or strong (bidirectional total variation Lipschitz) conditions lead to different results. We prove sharpness under the strong condition and show that this condition covers, as a special case, distributions having a positive Lipschitz density.

title: Urheberrechtsverletzung durch Memorisierung und Output von Musikwerken in KI‑Systemen
abstract: Zusammenfassung Gegenstand des Rechtstreits vor dem LG München I war eine Klage der Verwertungsgesellschaft GEMA gegen die Anbieterin eines KI‑Systems wegen Urheberrechtsverletzungen, weil die Anbieterin in ihrem KI‑System Melodien bekannter Künstler wiedergibt, die von der GEMA vertreten werden, ohne mit der GEMA einen Lizenzvertrag abgeschlossen zu haben. Das Gericht erörtert auf 137 Seiten mit 559 Randziffern ausführlich wichtige urheberrechtliche Rechtsfragen im Hinblick auf die Nutzung des KI‑Systems. Die Entscheidung des Gerichts beruht nicht nur auf deutschem bzw. europäischem, sondern auch auf US‑amerikanischem Recht, weil das Gericht sich hierzu aufgrund einer besonderen Zuständigkeitsregelung im Verwertungsgesellschaftengesetz (VGG) berechtigt bzw. verpflichtet sieht.

title: Securing Enterprise Language Model Applications Against Data Leakage and Response Manipulation
abstract: Enterprise language-model applications combine internal documents, retrieval, conversation history, and executable tools. This critical narrative and thematic review examines data leakage and response manipulation through targeted discovery completed on September 29, 2026, with a bounded supplementary discovery and source-status audit on October 1, 2026. Primary studies are distinguished from institutional guidance and contextual reviews. The evidence identifies indirect prompt injection, corpus poisoning, retrieval-stage exploitation, log contamination, embedding inversion, and cumulative knowledge-base extraction under different conditions (Chang et al., 2026; Greshake et al., 2023; Morris et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2026). Defensive studies address provenance signaling, structured training, preference optimization, capability enforcement, and action attribution, with configuration-dependent findings (Chen, Piet, et al., 2025; Chen, Zharmagambetov, et al., 2025; Debenedetti et al., 2026; He et al., 2026). The synthesis proposes six assurance boundaries: identity and scope, source authorization, content provenance, model interaction, executable actions, and output release. Provider and inference-data handling, monitoring, and incident response span all six. Authoritative confidentiality and authorization decisions require application or infrastructure controls independent of unconstrained model interpretation. The framework is an author-developed, unvalidated decision aid, not a certification or a NIST/OWASP-endorsed standard. A hypothetical assistant and prospective protocol illustrate permission-preserving processing, cumulative-disclosure budgets, revocation propagation, legitimate-task utility, and verification effort. No original experiment, complete database census, or universal estimate of compromise is claimed.
